gadkhali-flower-fields.desc: Around Gadkhali in Jhikargachha, farmers grow flowers instead of rice, and in winter the fields glow red, yellow and white. Marigold, tuberose, rose, gerbera and gladiolus are cut every morning and sold at a roadside wholesale market before being trucked to Dhaka and other cities. Demand peaks before Pohela Falgun, Valentine's Day and Ekushey February. Walking the field paths with farmers at work is the joy of it.
blocks: How to get there
Buses towards Benapole from Jashore stop at Gadkhali bazar (about 30–40 min).
Good to know
Go early to see the morning flower market; ask farmers before entering fields and don't pick flowers.

glance: 180 km to Jashore by road, 5–6 hours by bus or car
chanchra-shiva-temple.desc: The Chanchra Shiva Temple was built by the Chanchra zamindars in the 1690s, in the curved-roof aat-chala style. Its front is covered with terracotta work showing floral designs and figures. It is a protected monument and one of the better surviving examples of temple art in the region. The Chanchra Rajbari ruins are close by.
blocks: How to get there
A rickshaw or auto from Jashore town centre to Chanchra on the Khulna road.
Good to know
Morning light is best for photographing the terracotta.

glance: About 7 BDT per luchi and 15 BDT for a plate of dal or vegetables (2025)
Joljog, Chowrasta, Deshbandhu Chittaranjan Road (Rail Road), beside Kotwali Police Station, Jashore town
joljog-luchi-jashore.desc: Kalipada Biswas opened Joljog in 1893, and it is still where much of Jashore town starts its day. From first light it fries luchi to order, served with dal in the morning and mixed vegetables in the evening. The counter also holds chomchom, kalojam, roshmalai, mihidana and pera sandesh; in winter the jhola gur sweets go fastest. It stays busy from dawn until night and is one of the cheapest breakfasts in town.
blocks: Good to know
Go early in the morning for the freshest luchi.

glance: Sweet shops at Jamtala bazar, Sharsha
jamtala-rosogolla.desc: On the road to Benapole, the market town of Jamtala in Sharsha is known for its rosogolla. The chhana balls are soft and spongy, soaked in light syrup. Travellers to and from the border often stop to eat and carry clay pots home. Try them fresh and warm if you can.

glance: 180 km to Jashore by road, 5–6 hours by bus or car
jhanpa-baor.desc: Jhanpa (also called Rajganj) Baor is a horseshoe-shaped lake left behind by an old river course in Manirampur upazila. It is listed as the main sight of the upazila. Villagers built a floating bridge across it on rows of drums, and walking over the water on it has made the baor a popular outing for families. Boat races are held on the lake. Late afternoon, with the light low over the water, is the nicest time.
blocks: How to get there
Bus from Jashore to Manirampur (about 45 minutes), then an easy bike to Rajganj bazar and Jhanpa village.
Good to know
The floating bridge moves underfoot; hold children's hands and avoid it when crowded or in strong wind. Ask locals about the boat race dates.

glance: 180 km to Jashore by road, 5–6 hours by bus or car
benapole-border.desc: Benapole in Sharsha upazila faces Petrapole in India, and the road from here reaches Kolkata in about 80 km. It is the largest land port in Bangladesh, and most travellers to and from Kolkata cross here by bus, car or the Bandhan Express train. The approach is lined with long queues of lorries, money changers and transport offices, which is a show in itself. Each evening the border guards of both countries hold a flag-lowering ceremony at the zero line that draws spectators. Benapole was also the headquarters of Sector 8 in the Liberation War.
blocks: How to get there
Buses and local trains run from Jashore to Benapole (about 1 hour); an easy bike takes you from the bus stand to the checkpost.
Good to know
Carry photo ID; you can only go up to the zero line with a passport and visa. Ceremony timing depends on sunset, so ask the BGB post on the day.

bharat-bhayna.desc: Bharat Bhayna is an archaeological mound near the Bhadra river in Keshabpur. Excavation exposed a massive brick structure with many cells, thought to be an early medieval Buddhist temple base. It stands in open countryside and sees few visitors. Combine it with a trip to Sagardari.
blocks: How to get there
From Keshabpur, hire an auto or bike; ask for Bharat Bhayna or Bharat Rajar Deul.
Good to know
No facilities on site; wear a hat and carry water.

jashore-institute-library.desc: The library was founded in 1851, making it the oldest in the country and one of the oldest in South Asia. In 1927 it was merged with the Aryan Theatre and the Town Club to form the Jashore Institute, and the town grew up around it, with the Town Hall built in 1904. During the Second World War the Royal Indian Air Force took over the compound. Today it holds over 67,000 books in Bangla and English. A short stop in the middle of town for anyone who loves old institutions.
blocks: How to get there
It is in the town centre near Dhaka Road; a rickshaw from anywhere in Jashore town.
Good to know
Go during opening hours, keep quiet in the reading room, and ask staff before taking photos.

glance: Approx. 300–500 BDT per kg for good patali
Weekly gur haats around Jashore and village tappers in Chougachha and Bagharpara
jashore-khejur-gur.desc: Jashore is the best-known home of khejur gur. In winter, tappers called gachhi cut the date palms and hang clay pots to catch the sweet sap overnight. The sap is boiled down in large pans into runny jhola gur or set into patali cakes. Its smoky caramel taste goes into payesh, pitha and nolen gur sweets across Bengal.

jashore-embroidery.desc: The Jashore stitch is a style of dense, colourful hand embroidery done on cotton and silk. Thousands of rural women work on contract for local businesses, filling borders and yokes with flowers, vines and geometric patterns. Finished pieces are sold across the country and in boutiques in Dhaka. Shops in Jashore town sell directly at better prices.

glance: 180 km to Jashore by road, 5–6 hours by bus or car
sagardari-madhusudan-home.desc: Michael Madhusudan Dutt, pioneer of Bengali blank verse and the sonnet, was born at Sagardari in Keshabpur in 1824. His family home is now a museum with memorabilia and a statue in the courtyard. Nearby, the Kopotakkho river, celebrated in his sonnet, flows slowly past. A large fair gathers here every January for his birth anniversary.
blocks: How to get there
Bus from Jashore to Keshabpur (about 1 hr), then an auto or van to Sagardari.
Good to know
Visit during the Madhu Mela in late January for music and stalls, or on a weekday for quiet.

madhu-mela.desc: Every year around the poet's birth anniversary on 25 January, Sagardari hosts the Madhu Mela. The poet's home becomes the centre of recitations, songs and discussions about his work. Around it grows a classic village fair with sweets, toys, pottery and rides. It draws crowds from across the south-west.
blocks: Good to know
Weekends are very crowded; arrive in the morning.
